questions.q: What does a ReplicaSet do when you change the container image in its `template` and reapply?
options: Nothing happens to already-running Pods — a ReplicaSet has no rollout logic
It immediately replaces all running Pods with the new image
It deletes all Pods and refuses to create new ones
It automatically creates a Deployment
questions.explain: A ReplicaSet's job is only to maintain a count of Pods matching its selector. It has no concept of rolling out a template change to already-running Pods — that gap is what Deployment exists to close.

questions.q: What does a Deployment actually manage directly?
options: Nodes in the cluster
Pods, directly, bypassing ReplicaSets entirely
ReplicaSets — it creates new ones for template changes and manages scaling them up/down
Only the container images, not Pods or ReplicaSets
questions.explain: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets, not Pods directly. When the Pod template changes, it creates a new ReplicaSet, scales it up, and scales the old one down.

questions.q: After updating a Deployment's image and running `kubectl get rs`, you see two ReplicaSets: one at 3/3 and one at 0/0. What does this mean?
options: The old ReplicaSet is scaled to zero and kept for rollback history, while the new one is running at full strength
Both ReplicaSets are currently serving live traffic
Kubernetes created a duplicate Deployment by mistake
The deployment failed and needs to be deleted
questions.explain: Deployments keep old ReplicaSets around, scaled to zero, specifically to support rollback — this is normal, expected behavior after a successful rollout.

questions.q: What is the main downside of scaling with `kubectl scale deployment checkout --replicas=10` compared to editing the YAML's `spec.replicas` and reapplying?
options: It's imperative and leaves no record in version control, unlike editing the file and reapplying through Git
It permanently deletes the Deployment
kubectl scale does not actually work on Deployments
It can only scale down, never up
questions.explain: kubectl scale is a quick, one-off imperative command with no tracked history. Editing spec.replicas in a YAML file kept in Git and reapplying is reviewable and reproducible.

questions.q: Why do you create Deployment objects directly instead of ReplicaSet objects, even though Deployments use ReplicaSets underneath?
options: A Deployment creates and owns its ReplicaSets automatically, adding safe rollout/rollback logic that a bare ReplicaSet lacks
ReplicaSets can only be created by an administrator, never by a regular user
ReplicaSet YAML is not valid in modern Kubernetes versions
Deployments and ReplicaSets are functionally identical, so it doesn't matter
questions.explain: Deployment is the higher-level interface: it manages ReplicaSets automatically and adds rollout/rollback behavior that ReplicaSet alone does not provide.
